title: Sentence-final 'way' token
description: This latent fires on the word "way" occurring at or near the end of a sentence or clause, often as part of phrases like "in a ... way," "the right way," or "that way." It appears to track a specific lexical/positional pattern rather than any particular topic, activating whenever this common noun closes out a clause, especially in constructions describing manner or method. It would not activate on other uses of "way" mid-sentence embedded in unrelated syntax, nor on synonyms like "manner" or "method," nor on sentences that lack this specific closing token pattern.

title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on the numeral (and optional bold markdown asterisks) that begins an item in a numbered list, such as '2.', '3. **', or '14', typically at the start of a line enumerating points, steps, options, or pros/cons. It activates on the marker token itself regardless of the list's topic, whether it's steps in advice, reasons, options, or sub-points, and fires most strongly on bare digit-plus-punctuation tokens with or without bold formatting. It would not activate on ordinary prose sentences lacking list structure, on bullet points using symbols like '-' or '*' instead of numerals, or on the introductory line preceding a list (e.g. 'Here's why:') that itself contains no numeral marker.

title: Terse directive or evaluative assertion
description: This latent fires on short, self-contained declarative or imperative sentences that deliver a firm directive, judgment, or refusal rather than descriptive or narrative content. Examples include list-item instructions ('Make a conscious effort...', 'Expand your social circle'), curt evaluative verdicts ('Her second reason is more concerning.', 'You just assumed it was real...'), flat section-header nouns ('Credit'), and blunt refusal statements ('I cannot continue...'). The common thread is brevity combined with an assertive, closing-the-topic tone -- the sentence functions as a compact command, verdict, or boundary-setting statement rather than elaborating or explaining. It would not activate on longer explanatory, descriptive, or hedged sentences that build an argument gradually rather than delivering a terse conclusive statement.

title: Instruction to be direct
description: This latent activates on phrases instructing someone to avoid indirectness, hedging, or evasive communication, such as 'avoid beating around the bush' or similar directives to be blunt and get to the point. It fires on imperative language that frames directness/conciseness as a desired behavior, often in the context of advice, instructions, or communication guidelines. It would not activate on sentences that merely describe someone being indirect or evasive without framing it as an instruction, nor on general statements about honesty or clarity that lack the imperative 'avoid/don't do X vague behavior' structure.

title: Retracting a joking statement
description: This latent fires on phrases where the speaker signals that a preceding statement was made in jest and is being retracted or clarified as not serious, often using markers like 'just kidding' or 'I won't actually...'. It activates on self-correcting, playful asides that undercut or negate a prior claim for comedic or rapport-building effect. It would not activate on straightforward jokes without a retraction, sincere statements, or corrections that aren't framed as humor (e.g., factual clarifications lacking a playful tone).

title: Hedging / tentative suggestion markers
description: This latent fires on hedge words like "Maybe" or "Perhaps" that introduce a tentative suggestion, alternative, or uncertain claim, typically at the very start of a sentence or clause. It activates on the lexical marker itself rather than on the content that follows, capturing the linguistic gesture of softening a statement or proposing an option without full commitment. It would not activate on confident, declarative assertions, factual statements, or sentences expressing uncertainty through other means (e.g., "I'm not sure" or "It could be argued") that lack these specific hedge tokens at the outset.
